extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of comic, digressive 18th-century style fiction; literature students studying narrative voice and satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards for composing satirical, digressive comic prose exemplified by Tristram Shandy: choices about tone, digression, small incidents, irony, learned parody, and narratorly intrusion. Useful for writers modeling or analyzing comic, erudite narrative voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid displaying learning in place of substance
rubrics_metrics.description: “To preach, to shew the extent of our reading, or the subtleties of our wit—to parade in the eyes of the vulgar with the beggarly accounts of a little learning...—is a dishonest use of the poor single half hour in a week which is put into our hands—’Tis not preaching the gospel—but ourselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute ostentation of learning for meaningful content; avoid using demonstration of erudition as the primary purpose of a speech/piece. The persuasive power should come from sincerity and effect on the audience, not from flaunting references or 'tinsel'd' words that glitter but convey little light or warmth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct address to the heart (directness over display)
rubrics_metrics.description: “For my own part... I had rather direct five words point-blank to the heart.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise, emotionally direct statements over long, elaborate conceits when the aim is to move or persuade. A few well-chosen words that hit the reader emotionally are preferable to verbose displays of wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid glittering words that lack substance
rubrics_metrics.description: a few words which glitter, but convey little light and less warmth
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of rhetorical embellishments that sound impressive but lack meaning; stylistic ornament should serve insight or feeling rather than impressiveness alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small incidents (trifles) to produce large effects
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is curious to observe the triumph of slight incidents over the mind... that trifles, light as air, shall waft a belief into the soul.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy seemingly trivial actions or details (a roasted chesnut, a dropped gesture) to catalyze belief, misapprehension, character development, or plot shifts. Trifles can credibly change opinions and carry narrative weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit ambiguity between public mask and private intention (double-voiced gestures)
rubrics_metrics.description: “You must mark and carefully separate and distinguish these two things in your mind. —The smile was for the company. —The threat was for Yorick.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft moments where a character's public expression differs from private intent; use subtle gestures or tone to carry dual meanings and let readers infer the private stance beneath the public façade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let character temperament determine whether they correct reputational wrongs
rubrics_metrics.description: Yorick’s ‘singularity of his temper’ would never suffer him to take pains to set a story right... he trusted to time and truth to do it for him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect and use consistent character flaws (pride, stubbornness, hauteur) as drivers of plot and ongoing misinterpretations; characters need not always act to correct misunderstandings—such omissions can define them and generate consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical comedy to satirize ideas or reputations
rubrics_metrics.description: The hot chesnut falling into Phutatorius’s breeches was read as a ‘sarcastical fling’ at his book; physical accident becomes allegory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage bodily or comic mishaps that readers can interpret as symbolic commentary on a character's work, opinions, or reputation. Physical gags can double as satirical statements about ideas or authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ learned digressions and mock-authority for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthy pseudo-legal, canonical, and learned debates (e.g., whether a mother is 'of kin' to her child; citations of Brook, Lord Coke, Swinburn) and pedantic medical/printing prescriptions are used for humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody pedantry by inserting erudite-sounding discussions, citations, and technical minutiae; the contrast between solemn authority and comic absurdity produces satire. Use footnotes, asides, and formal references to heighten mock-legal or mock-scientific tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use musical/metaphoric language to register tone mismatches
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers ‘who had very nice ears’ could distinguish the mixed tones as plainly as a third or a fifth; the concord was good but 'quite out of the key' and not applicable to the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply musical or sensory metaphors to describe tonal dissonance in speech or scene; metaphors can make mismatched affect tangible and amusing to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withhold information (postpone disclosure) to build anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: “In short, I’ll tell it in the next chapter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deliberate delays in revealing details as a structural and comic device—teasing readers with promises and holding back content to heighten curiosity and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let small gestures drive inference and misattribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Phutatorius infers from Yorick picking up the chesnut that Yorick had originally slipped it in—small action becomes basis for wide belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage tiny, ambiguous actions that other characters will over-interpret; such misattributions are a fertile source of misunderstanding, conflict, and plot advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody scientific/medical pretension through absurd specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: The mock-prescription of using a fresh printed leaf (oil and lamp-black in the type) with an argument about type-size and 'sanative particles' spread 'infinitely thin' to effect cure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirize professional authority by couching ridiculous remedies in pseudo-technical language. Specificity and faux-precision lend credibility to absurd claims, amplifying comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratorial intrusion and meta-commentary as structural voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator frequently interrupts with comments: 'It is not my business to dip my pen in this controversy', 'I will endeavour to explain to you with all imaginable decency', and other authorial asides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a conversational, self-aware narrator who interrupts, comments, and directly addresses readers. Such intrusions shape tone, guide interpretation, and create a distinctive, intimate voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical/allusive references to create comic erudition
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent references to authorities like Montaigne, Euclid, Hippocrates, Selden, Lord Coke, Latin maxims, and mock-Latin citations enliven disputes and satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sprinkle classical and learned allusions to contrast the narrator's or characters' erudition with the triviality or absurdity of the subject; the gap between reference and situation yields humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure narrative through deliberate digressions and chapter-teasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring device of tearing chapters, interrupting sentences, and promising to continue 'in the next chapter', making digression itself a feature: 'And so much for tearing out of chapters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make digressions a formal, expected part of the work—use interruptions, parenthetical remarks, and chapter-level teasing to shape rhythm and reader expectation, turning side-tracks into a primary stylistic device.
